look_here_first: COMPOSITE DROPSEED (perennial): look for the tall, tight to somewhat spreading slender flowering head and lasting basal clump. It can look almost identical to S. clandestinus; the key is mature grains and lemma anatomy, not tallness or an open panicle. Species-rank native/range record stays as already approved; disputed variety concepts are separate.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Latest B043 deep review supports Hays at accepted species rank through var. drummondii, Bexar ecological-site documentation, and Kerr field-succession evidence.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Install and label at species rank. Strict var. compositus Travis material remains disputed and is not used for the PASS decision.

best_field_traits: perennial bunchgrass, substantially taller and more robust than annual poverty dropseed
panicle long and narrow, varying from contracted to somewhat open
spikelets small and numerous along slender panicle branches
persistent perennial crown separates it quickly from annual Sporobolus vaginiflorus
crew_field_check: Perennial bunchgrass with narrow crowded panicles. Distinguish from S. clandestinus by measured glumes/lemmas and fresh mature seed pericarp typically becoming gelatinous and slipping off the seed after wetting; a narrow head alone cannot separate the two. Against S. vaginiflorus, rooted duration and spikelet studies matter.
1-flowered, awnless Sporobolus spikelets — not the multi-flowered bristled clusters of Setaria/Cenchrus.
Photographs of head outline are first clues, NOT confirmed lemma/pericarp identification.
Anther/flower color, panicle width and small/large height alone are not safe identifications.

lookalikes.difference: Also perennial, but rough dropseed is typically recognized by its narrower contracted panicle and rough-textured spikelets; check spikelet pubescence and texture rather than relying on height alone.
Poverty dropseed is an annual, generally smaller, and produces cleistogamous flowers hidden in the upper leaf sheaths.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Check fully mature caryopsis and lemma; preserve whole-plant crown evidence.
field_matrix.difference: Both perennial and similarly headed. Composite dropseed tends to have gelatinizing, separating seed pericarp on fresh wet grains versus persistent/non-gelatinizing in S. clandestinus.
field_matrix.guardrail: The species-complex and varieties have documented identification disagreements; avoid mapping a cultivar/variety from a silhouette.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Compare rooted duration and terminal/axillary panicles.
field_matrix.difference: Annual poverty dropseed frequently has concealed upper-sheath flowering; composite is a perennial and may ALSO form axillary enclosed spikelets.
field_matrix.guardrail: Hidden sheath flowering is not exclusively S. vaginiflorus.

not_reliable_alone: Presence of hidden sheath flowers (multiple related dropseeds can have these)
Being taller/shorter or open/contracted at a single drought-stressed moment
Claiming a micro-lemma character from an ordinary phone photograph

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Dropseed — what can this photograph really identify?
steps: Check whether the photographed plant includes a ROOTED base: annual or perennial is NOT proven by an unrooted picture.
Follow the flowering axis into a true one-flowered dropseed spikelet. These panicles can look similar across species.
Search the upper leaf SHEATH for enclosed axillary flowers, but do not use this as an exclusive S. vaginiflorus test.
Measure fresh mature spikelets and inspect the lemma; compare fresh grain pericarp only if separating the S. compositus complex.
If no mature flowers, true crown or measured seed characters, identify only Sporobolus sp. or tentative complex.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Use visible macro morphology first and defer difficult perennial-species separations to mature material, reliable grain tests and microscope when necessary.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Do not mistake labels and source IDs for independently confirmed Hays vouchers; exact microscope and concealed flower photographs remain missing.
